profile.reading: This point in Lufkin, in Angelina County, Texas, near an address on Brentwood Drive, is named Precision Prints Lufkin Datacenter. Precision Prints appears to be a small local printing business, and the word Datacenter attached to its name most plausibly describes that company's own in house server room or IT closet used to run design, printing, and order management systems, rather than a commercial data center that leases space or connectivity to outside customers. Small businesses in many industries keep a closet or small room of servers and networking equipment to run their own operations, and such rooms are sometimes labeled in mapping data with the same tag used for genuine wholesale and retail data centers, which can make the two hard to tell apart without more information. No working website or independent business listing could be found for Precision Prints at this address to verify the scale of its computing equipment. Based on the business name and the small East Texas residential setting, this is filed as a probable small in house server closet rather than a commercial data center operation, and no capacity or specification figures are published for it.

reading.body:
One of Texas's 133 mapped data center facilities is a print shop's server closet, and it contributes nothing to the 468 megawatts the state's facilities publish.

The point in Lufkin, in Angelina County, carries the same data center tag as a wholesale facility, but its name belongs to a small local printing business. The most plausible reading is an in-house server room running design, printing, and order management systems. No website resolves at the address, no independent listing confirms any computing footprint, and no capacity figures are published. The tag does not distinguish between a building that leases space and power to tenants and a closet that runs one company's email.

Texas has 133 mapped facilities, of which 18 publish power capacity, summing to 468 megawatts. Counting buildings and counting power give very different pictures of the same state. For AI workload placement, the number that matters is megawatts, and megawatts are only visible where an operator publishes them. A site like this one is absent from that total, correctly, because it has nothing to add to it.

What the data does not establish is how much data center capacity Texas actually holds, only how much is published. It does not show whether the unpublished remainder is large or small. It also says nothing about grid interconnection or power supply in the state, because no such information is attached to this point.
